---
title: "Cognitive interviews with language models"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5,
                      dpi = 96, out.width = "100%")
```

This tutorial runs simulated cognitive interviews: A
language model plays each persona you define, thinks aloud while it answers
a survey item, and then answers the verbal probes a cognitive interviewer
would ask. A second call codes each transcript for problems. The result is
a list of items and wording worth a closer look, most useful when you have
no real respondents yet, for example right after a synthetic pretest.

It is a **screening aid**. A model does not remember its own life or feel
uncomfortable, so it cannot stand in for cognitive interviews with real
people or for a field test. Use it to decide what to bring to those.

Everything below runs with the **mock** provider, which gives canned
transcripts without calling an API. Swap in `sc_model("anthropic")`,
`sc_model("openai")` or `sc_model("ollama", ...)` for a real run.

```{r}
library(synthcheck)
```

## 1. The protocol

Each interview is one conversation with one persona about one item. It
follows the usual mix of think-aloud and scripted probes in cognitive
interviewing (Willis, 2005; Beatty & Willis, 2007):

1. **Think-aloud and answer.** The persona reads the statement, says what
   goes through its mind and answers on the scale.
2. **Probes.** The persona answers the probes from `sc_probes()` in the same
   conversation.
3. **Coding.** A separate call with no persona reads the transcript and
   codes problems at the four stages of answering a survey question
   (Tourangeau, 1984): Comprehension, retrieval, judgement and response
   mapping, plus sensitivity. For each it gives a yes or no and a note with
   a quote, then an overall severity and a suggested rewording.

The default probes:

```{r}
sc_probes()
```

Write your own with `stage` and `probe`, for example a shorter protocol:

```{r}
sc_probes(stage = c("comprehension", "comprehension", "response"),
          probe = c("In your own words, what is this statement asking?",
                    "What does 'rules' mean to you here?",
                    "Was it easy to pick a number?"))
```

`sc_interview_prompts()` shows exactly what is sent for one item:

```{r}
h <- hexaco_items[hexaco_items$trait == "H", ]
h <- h[seq(1, nrow(h), by = 4), ]   # ten items across the four facets
h$trait <- "Honesty-Humility"
ins <- sc_instrument(h, scale = c(1, 7), name = "HEXACO Honesty-Humility")
ins
p <- sc_interview_prompts(ins, h$item[1], "You are a 34-year-old nurse in Calgary.")
cat(p$system)
cat(p$think_aloud)
cat(p$probes)
```

## 2. Personas

Choose personas that differ as much as your future respondents will: Age,
education, first language, reading level, and anything the items touch on.
Varied personas are what make the interviews useful.

```{r}
per <- sc_persona_grid(
  age = c(19, 45, 72),
  education = c("did not finish high school", "has a university degree"),
  template = "You are a {age}-year-old adult in Canada who {education}.")
per
```

## 3. Run the interviews

```{r}
iv <- cognitive_interview(ins, list(sc_model("mock", name = "Model A"),
                                    sc_model("mock", name = "Model B")),
                          per, coder = sc_model("mock", name = "Coder"), interviews = 2,
                          progress = FALSE)
iv
```

The message gives the number of interviews and requests (three per
interview) before anything is sent. This run, with two models, six personas,
ten items and two interviews each, is 240 interviews, which costs little on
the default models. All 240 HEXACO items would be 24 times more, so start
with the items you are least sure of.

Use a different model as `coder` in real runs, so that no model grades its
own interviews. Two or more respondent models also help: Personas from one
model tend to sound alike.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
iv <- cognitive_interview(ins, list(sc_model("anthropic"), sc_model("openai")), per,
                          coder = sc_model("anthropic", "claude-sonnet-5-5"),
                          parallel = 4, output = "interviews_honesty")
```

With `output`, the table is saved with `run.json` and one Markdown file of
transcripts per item in `transcripts/`, which is the easiest way to read
them.

## 4. Summarise per item

```{r}
s <- summarise_interviews(iv)
s
```

Each row is one item: The share of interviews with a problem at each stage
and at any stage, how many personas and models raised one, the stage that
drives it, and the coder's most common notes and rewordings. An item is
flagged when at least 30% of its interviews found a problem (change it with
`flag`) and, with two or more models, at least two models found one.

```{r}
s[s$flagged, c("item", "statement", "top_stage", "notes", "revisions")]
```

## 5. One picture

```{r}
gg_interview(s)
```

Rows are items, with the most problems at the top. Pale is no problem,
red is a problem in most interviews, and an asterisk marks a flagged item.

## 6. Read the transcripts

The codes point to where to look; the transcripts show why:

```{r}
one <- iv[iv$item == s$item[1], ][1, ]
cat(one$think_aloud, "\n\n")
cat(one$probe_paraphrase, "\n")
cat(one$comprehension_note, "\n")
```

## 7. After a pretest

The pretest is optional: Without one, the interviews cover all items, or
the ones you name in `items`. When you have run a synthetic pretest, pass its result as `pretest`. The
interviews then cover the flagged items (most often flagged first), and each
gets one more probe aimed at the reason for its flag: A weak link to its
scale becomes "Does this statement seem to be about the same thing as
statements about Honesty-Humility?", a near-duplicate becomes "Does this
statement seem to ask the same thing as another statement?", and so on.
A data frame with `item` and `flag` columns works too:

```{r}
flags <- data.frame(item = h$item[c(5, 2)],
                    flag = c("Weak link to its scale", "Reverse key not working"))
iv2 <- cognitive_interview(ins, list(sc_model("mock", name = "Model A"),
                                     sc_model("mock", name = "Model B")),
                           per, pretest = flags, interviews = 2, progress = FALSE)
summarise_interviews(iv2)
```

`agreement` says whether an item was flagged by both the pretest and the
interviews, by one of them, or by neither. Items flagged by both are the
first to revise.

## In the app

The app runs the same interviews on screen. On the About tab, answer **No,
not yet** to the first question, and the app adds an **Interviews** tab (5)
after the Pretest tab. It uses the personas and models of the Personas and
Models tabs, interviews the items the pretest flagged or items you choose,
lets you edit the probes and pick the coder, and shows the summary, the
heatmap and the transcripts. See [the tour of the app](app-tour.html#interviews-without-real-data).

## What the interviews can and cannot tell you

- **Most useful:** Comprehension and response mapping. Vague words,
  double negatives, two questions in one, or a scale that fits poorly show up
  in the paraphrases and the probes.
- **Least useful:** Retrieval and judgement. A model guesses what such a
  person might say; it has no memories to search.
- **Too easy:** Models understand items better than many real respondents,
  so an item without problems here is not shown to work.
- **Too alike:** Personas played by one model sound alike. More models and
  more varied personas help, but do not fix it.

The interviews choose what to take to cognitive interviews with real people
and a field test. They do not replace either.

## References

- Beatty, P. C., & Willis, G. B. (2007). Research synthesis: The practice of
  cognitive interviewing. *Public Opinion Quarterly, 71*(2), 287-311.
- Tourangeau, R. (1984). Cognitive science and survey methods. In T. Jabine,
  M. Straf, J. Tanur & R. Tourangeau (Eds.), *Cognitive aspects of survey
  methodology: Building a bridge between disciplines* (pp. 73-100). National
  Academy Press.
- Willis, G. B. (2005). *Cognitive interviewing: A tool for improving
  questionnaire design.* Sage.
- Willis, G. B., & Lessler, J. T. (1999). *Question Appraisal System QAS-99.*
  Research Triangle Institute.
